title: Two boys rescued from Venezuela earthquake rubble after days of being trapped
summary_cn: 委内瑞拉在遭受两次强烈地震后，救援人员于周日从废墟中救出33人，其中包括两名11岁男孩。尽管已过72小时黄金救援期，但仍有数万人失踪，救援工作因余震和物资匮乏而受阻。国际救援队已抵达协助，但部分受灾地区清理工作尚未开始。
paragraphs_en: This video can not be played
An 11-year-old boy, named Moises, was rescued after days trapped beneath heavy rubble
More stories of miraculous rescue have emerged from Venezuela on Sunday, days after two powerful earthquakes struck the country.

Interim President Delcy RodrÃ­guez said 33 people had been pulled from debris alive over the weekend. Among them were two 11-year-old boys, who were separately rescued from collapsed buildings within hours of each other on Sunday.
However, with tens of thousands of people still missing, hopes of finding more survivors are fading by the hour.
Aid agencies say the first 48 to 72 hours after a disaster are crucial for finding people alive. Relatives of the missing are facing a fifth night waiting for news of their loved ones.
Since the magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 quakes on Wednesday, officials have confirmed at least 1,450 deaths.

The two earthquakes, which struck within 39 seconds, caused hundreds of buildings to collapse and many people remain trapped inside. Desperate families have been digging through the debris by hand, trying to find their loved ones.
Some have told the BBC that they can hear people under the rubble , but cannot move the heavy slabs of concrete, and are waiting anxiously for heavy machinery to arrive.
Though the crucial 72-hour window had passed, rescuers had not given up on Sunday, saying people could still be found alive, especially if they had access to food and water.
RodrÃ­guez has been sharing optimistic messages on social media, including videos of rescues from over the weekend.
Rescuers shared video footage of an 11-year-old boy, named as Moises, being pulled from twisted debris - his eyes covered to protect them from the sun.
11-year-old Moises was pulled out of the rubble after being trapped for days

Colombia's National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD) said Moises was buried under about 3m (9.8ft) of debris, and the rescue team spent six hours conducting "high-precision work" on Saturday to reach him.
Reuters reported that a rescuer was overheard on a walkie-talkie saying the young boy was found near his sister and mother, who had both died.
Hours later, RodrÃ­guez posted a video on X, purportedly showing the rescue of a second 11-year-old boy in the town of Caraballeda.
"In these hours, every life is hope for Venezuela," she wrote.
Also in Caraballeda, French and American teams rescued a father and his teenage son from under rubble on Sunday, news agency AFP reported.
Officials said the coastal region of La Guaira, where Caraballeda is located, has been hit the hardest.
Rescuers' efforts have been hampered by aftershocks, which are in turn terrifying residents.
"To be honest, it makes you feel kind of nervous. Any little noise... horrible," JesÃºs Andueza, a 64-year-old bus driver told BBC Mundo.

Frustration has also grown, with some saying the government's response is too slow and inefficient. In some of the worst areas, such as Caribe and Tanaguarena, there are entire areas where debris removal has not yet started.
One person told the BBC that the government was actually hindering rescue efforts, by limiting access to affected areas and closing roads.
Thousands of people are living in their cars or camping at places like the airport and golf course, away from buildings that could collapse.
The golf course in Caraballeda has become an epicentre for the emergency response.

Its green lawn, which used to be perfectly manicured, is now a makeshift hospital and donation centre, where residents who have lost everything are sifting through piles of donated clothing and boxes of humanitarian aid.

In another part of the golf course, next to a small lagoon, a strip of land has been set up as a landing pad for helicopters arriving with supplies and emergency personnel from within Venezuela and abroad.

In the area surrounding the golf course, Caraballeda's streets â cracked and covered in rubble â are marked by dust and silence, interrupted only by heavy machinery and those searching among the remains.

Watch: Inside the Venezuela country club that is now a makeshift hospital
Milagros GonzÃ¡lez, who lives in Caribe, told BBC Mundo that her building was one of the few that didn't collapse, and she fled as soon as she could to take refuge at the golf course.
"I left with my two young daughters and my two elderly relatives. But thank God we got out alive. The building can't be lived in. But we're alive, which is what matters," she said.
GonzÃ¡lez admitted that every time she lies down, she wakes up dizzy and thinks it's shaking.
"A psychologist just told me that it's part of the process," she said, while her two young daughters play with dolls on a mattress on the grass.
Donated clothes have been piling up at the Caraballeda golf course, for residents who have lost everything
In a separate video message on Sunday, RodrÃ­quez said the JosÃ© MarÃ­a Vargas sports complex in La Guaira was also serving as an emergency response centre.

Pointing out that the armed forces were sorting clothes, medicine and food, RodrÃ­guez said "everything is functioning as well as possible during these terrible moments, these terrible hours, that our people are enduring".

"Let them know that no one here is alone, not a single family or individual need [to] feel alone. Our people and our state are here, the social protection system is here, and international solidarity is here."
In recent days, international rescue teams from Mexico, Spain, Qatar, the US, and the UK have arrived to reinforce the search efforts.
The UN's Tom Fletcher said on Saturday that 39 search and rescue teams had been deployed from all over the world, with each consisting of 50-100 people.
"You're looking at almost 2,000 people surging in, 111 dogs, medical teams as well. We go in with these micro drones, they call them cockroach drones, that help us find people in the buildings."

一名叫莫伊塞斯（Moises）的11岁男孩在被困于厚重瓦砾下数天后获救
周日，委内瑞拉在遭受两次强烈地震数天后，又传出了更多奇迹般救援的故事。
临时总统德尔西·罗德里格斯（Delcy Rodríguez）表示，周末有33人从废墟中被活着救出。其中包括两名11岁男孩，他们在周日分别于几小时内从倒塌的建筑中被救出。
然而，由于仍有数万人失踪，找到更多幸存者的希望正随时间流逝而减弱。
援助机构表示，灾难发生后的头48至72小时是寻找生还者的关键时期。失踪者的亲属正面临第五个夜晚，等待亲人的消息。
自周三发生7.2级和7.5级地震以来，官员已确认至少1450人死亡。
这两次地震相隔39秒，导致数百栋建筑倒塌，许多人仍被困其中。绝望的家属们徒手挖掘废墟，试图找到他们的亲人。
一些人告诉BBC，他们能听到瓦砾下有人声，但无法移动沉重的混凝土板，正焦急等待重型机械到来。
尽管关键的72小时窗口已过，但救援人员周日并未放弃，称仍有可能找到生还者，尤其是如果他们能获得食物和水。
罗德里格斯一直在社交媒体上分享乐观信息，包括周末救援的视频。
救援人员分享了一段视频，显示一名叫莫伊塞斯的11岁男孩从扭曲的废墟中被拉出——他的眼睛被遮住以防阳光伤害。
11岁的莫伊塞斯在被困数天后从瓦砾中被救出
哥伦比亚国家灾害风险管理中心（UNGRD）表示，莫伊塞斯被埋在约3米（9.8英尺）深的废墟下，救援队周六花了六个小时进行“高精度作业”才到达他身边。
路透社报道，有人在对讲机中听到一名救援人员说，这名男孩是在他的姐姐和母亲附近被发现的，两人均已死亡。
几小时后，罗德里格斯在X上发布了一段视频，据称显示在卡拉巴列达（Caraballeda）镇救出了第二名11岁男孩。
她写道：“在这些时刻，每一条生命都是委内瑞拉的希望。”
据法新社报道，同样在卡拉巴列达，法国和美国救援队周日从废墟中救出了一名父亲和他十几岁的儿子。
官员表示，卡拉巴列达所在的拉瓜伊拉（La Guaira）沿海地区受灾最严重。
救援工作受到余震的阻碍，而余震又让居民感到恐惧。
64岁的公交车司机赫苏斯·安杜埃萨（Jesús Andueza）告诉BBC Mundo：“说实话，这让你感到有点紧张。任何一点小声音……都可怕。”
不满情绪也在增长，一些人表示政府的反应太慢且效率低下。在一些最严重的地区，如加勒比（Caribe）和塔纳瓜雷纳（Tanaguarena），整个区域的废墟清理尚未开始。
一人告诉BBC，政府实际上通过限制进入受灾地区和关闭道路来阻碍救援工作。
数千人住在自己的车里，或在机场和高尔夫球场等地露营，远离可能倒塌的建筑。
卡拉巴列达的高尔夫球场已成为应急响应的中心。
原本修剪整齐的绿色草坪现在变成了临时医院和捐赠中心，失去一切的居民正在翻捡成堆的捐赠衣物和人道主义援助物资箱。
在高尔夫球场的另一部分，靠近一个小泻湖的地方，一块区域被设为直升机停机坪，用于接收来自委内瑞拉国内外的物资和应急人员。
在高尔夫球场周边，卡拉巴列达的街道——开裂且覆盖着瓦砾——被尘土和寂静笼罩，只有重型机械和废墟中搜寻的人们打破这种氛围。

观看：委内瑞拉乡村俱乐部内部，如今成为临时医院
住在加勒比的米拉格罗斯·冈萨雷斯（Milagros González）告诉BBC Mundo，她的建筑是少数没有倒塌的之一，她尽快逃离并到高尔夫球场避难。
她说：“我带着两个年幼的女儿和两个年迈的亲戚离开了。但感谢上帝，我们活着出来了。那栋楼不能住了。但我们活着，这才是最重要的。”
冈萨雷斯承认，每次躺下，她都会头晕醒来，以为是地震。
她说：“一位心理学家刚刚告诉我，这是过程的一部分。”而她的两个小女儿正在草地上的床垫上玩娃娃。
捐赠的衣物在卡拉巴列达高尔夫球场堆积如山，供失去一切的居民使用。
在周日的另一段视频信息中，罗德里格斯表示，拉瓜伊拉的何塞·玛丽亚·巴尔加斯（José María Vargas）体育中心也作为应急响应中心运作。
罗德里格斯指出，武装部队正在分类衣物、药品和食物，她说：“在我们的人民正在忍受的这些可怕时刻、可怕时光里，一切都在尽可能好地运转。”
“让他们知道，这里没有人是孤独的，没有一个家庭或个人需要感到孤独。我们的人民和国家在这里，社会保障体系在这里，国际团结也在这里。”
近日，来自墨西哥、西班牙、卡塔尔、美国和英国的国际救援队已抵达，以加强搜救工作。
联合国汤姆·弗莱彻（Tom Fletcher）周六表示，已从世界各地部署了39支搜救队，每队由50至100人组成。
“你看到的是近2000人涌入，111只搜救犬，还有医疗队。我们带着这些微型无人机——他们称之为蟑螂无人机——进去，帮助我们找到建筑里的人。”
